item.title: Google Cloud Moves the Compute Engine API to Immutable Date-Based Versions
item.description:
Google Cloud has made date-based versioning of the Compute Engine API generally available, replacing the single mutable /v1 surface with immutable quarterly snapshots such as 2026-09-01, selected per request with a header or query parameter. New versions can change defaults, error formats, and IAM checks without touching /v1 callers, a model Azure Resource Manager and Stripe have used for years.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: M365 services slowly come back online after global outage
item.description:
After a lengthy Microsoft 365 outage disrupted business around the globe, Microsoft is now restoring services to its customers. As of 6:00 p.m. UTC (1 p.m. ET) on Friday, Nov. 13, Microsoft said that it is seeing broad recovery and stability across its services, although it is still reporting service degradation in Microsoft 365 services that interact with Exchange Online.

“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration,” the company said on its service health dashboard, noting that the global outage was not caused by a cyberattack or by AI.

It was, Microsoft said, a technical issue “introduced by an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.”

A long list of services has been unavailable or intermittently impacted since the outage began more than 24 hours ago. Currently, the company says that elements of Microsoft 365 products that interact with Exchange Online and email services may be affected in various ways, but components of that don’t rely on that interaction remain functional.

Aside from email itself, which may be delayed or inaccessible, some potentially unexpected products are suffering.

For example, users may not be able to load some Microsoft 365 Admin Center pages, and Cloud Update, Cloud Policy, and Inventory in Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center are affected. Users may not be able to load Copilot 365 Chat or receive responses from either the web version or the app, and Microsoft Intune device enrollment, device check-in, and device compliance policies “may have been intermittently impacted.” A long list of functions in Microsoft Purview and Microsoft Teams are impacted, and customers who have configured their Windows 365 tenant and Cloud PCs to use Microsoft Purview Customer Key for Windows 365 Cloud PCs may have users who are unable to connect to their Cloud PCs.

As well, users of Microsoft 365 apps such as Word or Excel may be unable to view recently used files.

A Microsoft update posted at 8:00 p.m. UTC (3 p.m. ET) said, “As infrastructure stabilizes, we’re still draining queued messages and rebalancing traffic, so customers may see improved sign-in/access while delivery and processing continue to catch up. We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet. Service access can recover before mail flow fully normalizes.”

Recovery from the outage creates opportunities for cyber criminals. Matt Hull, vice president of cyber intelligence and response at NCC Group, warned, “cyber criminals will be moving quickly to exploit the uncertainty, disruption and frustration that events like this create. Organizations should remind colleagues to be particularly vigilant, verify any unexpected contact through established channels before acting, and report anything suspicious without delay.”

He noted that social engineering is a particular concern, as attackers impersonate Microsoft or internal IT teams. “We could see attempts to convince people to reset passwords, approve multi-factor authentication requests or provide remote access to their devices,” he said.

Microsoft has promised a full post-incident report once its review is complete, and said in its status update,“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused you and your business. We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously.”

Related: Microsoft 365 caught a bug and the whole world sneezed

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.

item.title: Nvidia’s leadership crisis puts enterprise AI’s dependence on one company under scrutiny
item.description:
The tech world has been rattled by the toppling of one of its most prominent leaders, and the widespread implications it could have on the AI industry itself.

Nvidia, which provides the underlying AI infrastructure for seemingly every company on the planet, announced on Thursday that its president and CEO Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately. Earlier this week, news broke that Huang had had at least two extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with a direct report.

EVP and CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO, and Nvidia’s board has begun searching for a permanent replacement.

Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs) have become the standard for graphics rendering, and in recent years companies building AI have also depended on them for training and running large language models (LLMs) and increasingly sophisticated AI agents.

As such, the revelations about Huang, and his swift departure, have sparked a US national security crisis, and raised questions about over-reliance on one tech vendor and subsequent supply chain and compute constraints.

A scandal involving an admitted extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy opens up a hornet’s nest of concerns around security that Nvidia won’t be in a position to answer for months, if ever, said technology analyst Carmi Levy.

“More broadly, it throws into doubt the company’s leadership and security practices, and ignites questions around board-level governance and oversight,” he said.

The ‘default choice’ in the market

Huang founded Nvidia in 1993, initially targeting the gaming market. But the company pivoted in recent years to meet the intensive compute demands of AI. Its advanced GPUs not only excel at rendering graphics, but can handle an enormous number of simultaneous computations, making them a natural fit for neural networks and LLMs.

The company began focusing more on developing chips and architecture for AI tools and data centers, and has continued to ink new deals and establish partnerships with tech companies serving nearly every level of the stack, including Anthropic, Meta, Dell, HPE, Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Accenture, Marvell Technology, Hugging Face and many others.

“Nvidia has been the default choice for AI infrastructure buyers for as long as there’s been an AI infrastructure market,” Levy noted. There’s a reason it has hovered around 90% market share for so long, he said; it has been the lowest-risk choice for buyers whose success in their own roles depends on how effectively they minimize risk.

Personal relationships are creating real security risks

This chapter should serve as a wakeup call to corporate boards, Levy said, as it is their responsibility to mitigate risk on behalf of their organization and its stakeholders.

This is precisely what Nvidia’s board was doing amid rising concerns around reported Chinese targeting of senior corporate leaders, he pointed out. The board initiated an independent investigation into Huang’s actions earlier this week.

This should be a warning signal to other boards across the tech space that they “can’t afford to look the other way when human-factored risks hit their radar,” Levy said.

Emarketer senior analyst Asa Hiken agreed that Huang’s personal decisions raise much bigger questions about the security risks facing companies at the center of the AI race. “AI technology has become critical to US national security, making even the personal relationships of industry leaders a potential vulnerability,” he said.

IT buyers’ concerns post-resignation

As the saga continues to unfold, IT buyers may take a pause, Levy noted. Customers are leaning ever more heavily on AI platforms, making trust a greater factor in vendor choice. “Enterprises are now faced with the stark reality that the Nvidia of the future may not be the default choice that the Nvidia of the past has always been.”

There’s growing concern over the company’s ability to execute on its own roadmap; this could make it challenging for some customers to support their own internal delivery targets, Levy said. Changing vendors could mean major shifts in how they choose to build out their architectures, how they pay for them, and how they maintain them.

In the near term, a “hobbled” Nvidia could result in supply chain issues, component shortages, and project delays as the company struggles to regain its footing, Levy said.

Jack E. Gold, president and principal analyst at J.Gold Associates, agreed that there is some “real risk” that Huang’s leaving could hamper new technology deployments and create a bottleneck in R&D. The company has been able to define a very fast moving field through “sheer tech prowess” under his leadership.

This raises several questions: Will its ability to define the tech space be affected? Will Jensen leaving give Nvidia’s rivals an ability to catch up and perhaps exceed Nvidia, and thereby lessen its dominance?

“It wouldn’t happen immediately, but it could over time,” Gold said. 

Ultimately, though, Forrester VP Stephanie Balaouras advised, “tech leaders shouldn’t overreact, but they should treat Nvidia’s CEO transition as a prompt to reassess concentration risk across their AI infrastructure, suppliers, and investment plans.”

Nvidia’s troubles could promote more diversity in the IT stack

Longer term, though, the stage is set for improvements on all fronts as customers shift focus to other suppliers, and as competitors reposition themselves to serve an evolving market, Levy pointed out.

“A more diversified vendor landscape means customers may finally wean themselves off of this overly dominant provider,” he said.

However, it does come with near-term costs that enterprises should account for before they start planning their post-Jensen-Huang Nvidia relationship, he added. But ultimately, development could foreshadow a more robust AI ecosystem where chipmakers compete more aggressively, and one dominant player doesn’t set the tone for everyone else to follow.

“When a market is as dependent on a single player, as the Nvidia-led space so clearly has been, then it’s reasonable to conclude it was never sustainable to begin with,” Levy said.

This article was originally published on our sister publication Network World.

item.title: Saying no to AI spend is how we protect AI value
item.description:
It’s the 17th of the month and one of our engineers wants more credits for Claude. They’ve already spent $4,000 and we can’t believe it. Barely halfway through July and they’ve not only overshot their monthly budget but need an even larger allocation. Soon after, alerts start going out that we’ve reached 75% of our allocated monthly spend limit.

This request, among many others, made us think twice about AI spend. The interest is there and often the innovation is, too. But what about the value? If anyone asked us to approve an IT product that costs a few thousand dollars per seat, per month, would we say yes? Especially when the cost fluctuates and the return on investment isn’t guaranteed?

At Paessler, like many companies, we’re building the AI boat as we sail it. The trouble is that spend leaks are common in the wild waters of automation. We realized the need to correct course: value-vs-spend checks serve as a necessary compass and a cross-functional AI team keeps the ship structurally sound, preventing things like shadow AI or unchecked agents from sinking the budget.

We’ve learned the hard way that protecting AI value means being willing to sometimes say no, putting the processes and the people in place to make that call before the bill arrives. Heading into the new year, let’s explore why “tokenmaxxing” is out and “valuemaxxing” is in.

AI got a longer leash than any other software

Earlier this year, our first AI-focused dev day showed us just how quickly expenses can get out of hand. We offered a $5,000 prize for the best feature we could build into our network monitoring platform. The team loved it, resulting in a record 29 submissions, with some deliberately choosing more expensive approaches to build things that would otherwise have been impossible, ranging from context-aware assistants to root cause analysis helpers. We encouraged that experimentation and gave a very long leash on cost, precisely because we’d never done it before and wanted to see the outcome.

Despite some impressive applications, larger-than-expected invoices followed. More prompts meant more tokens and bigger bills, and agents doing multi-step work burned through credits even faster. Additionally, newer models became available, and the use of high effort levels began to send our bills to the stratosphere.

This is a familiar story. McKinsey reports that more than 9 out of 10 companies (93%) are exceeding their AI budgets. We’ve seen this anecdotally with another leader in our network, a CIO, who shared that their annual AI budget evaporated within two months. The one-two punch of AI being consumption-based and curiosity-driven is a dangerous combination for enterprise spend, especially as major providers are starting to meter heavy, agent-style usage separately. By 2028, Gartner predicts AI coding costs will overtake the average developer’s salary. In other words, the tools could cost more than the developer using them.

A spending cap is a decision, not a ban

Of course, we still want everyone to chase their wildest creative dreams with this technology, but it needs to happen in line with the cost reality. This means creating hard-and-fast rules like group limits. This needs to happen first because you can’t retrofit discipline onto a tool people already use freely. So, set the ceiling at rollout and make sure token limits align with spending limits.

We suggest finding the budget sweet spot by working backward. Figure out how much you’re comfortable spending per person or team and calculate from there. For some reason, many overlook this due diligence step in the race to automate. Other consumption-based tools never get as much leeway, so why AI? Treat it like any other resource by setting a maximum spend limit and raising it when the value shows up.

Done right, caps don’t get in the way of innovation. Rather, they’re a sense check between employee and employer, surfacing genuine use cases and ensuring alignment between spend and outcome.

For example, say an executive hits their monthly cap while performing heavy analysis before a board meeting. We don’t want to impede that critical work, especially when it’s time-sensitive, but we also want to keep an eye on who’s doing (and spending) what. A warning can evolve into a quick check and an increase. On the other hand, users may be experimenting with AI that isn’t yet tied to a critical business need. Again, a cap enables discussions and decisions, and in this case, a manager decides to pause spending. In both instances, the cap does its job and turns invisible outlay into a deliberate decision.

Saying no takes the right people in the room

It’s worth stressing that employees aren’t doing anything wrong. They’re understandably excited and legitimately experimenting, usually with positive results. But too much of a good thing can hit the bottom line. This is why the right culture is just as important as spend controls. If employees know to be cost-aware, they’ll be cost-aware, innovating within set limits and expectations.

The same goes for shadow AI. Ideally, employees shouldn’t onboard their own tools or duplicate processes across platforms, as it both wastes resources and creates an attack surface. But in reality, two-thirds of office professionals at large companies say they’ve used AI tools at work they believed weren’t permitted. The waste is one thing, paying for capability you don’t need or already own, but unmanaged exposure is another. Consolidation does double duty: cutting the spend and reducing the surface.

At Paessler, we try to catch such problems early by uniting around an AI Center of Excellence (CoE). This cross-functional group brings together decision makers from IT, information security, human resources, finance, legal and operational excellence, meeting weekly to safely and strategically scale AI adoption.

Before approving a new tool, we ask whether something we already pay for can do the job through an integration. New AI features are increasingly rolling out in software we use, so part of the work is simply keeping track of what’s already in our ecosystem. Once we know a feature exists, our pen tester also tries to break new AI apps by accessing data he shouldn’t be able to see.

Communicating more cost-effective ways of using AI can go a long way to prevent costly overruns and help users feel more in control. For example, Claude lets users select the amount of “effort” needed to answer a question or perform a task. More thorough responses require higher token usage and therefore higher cost. By educating employees, we can help them become more aware of model selection and adjust it based on their actual needs, not just a default setting.

The CoE is now our single voice on publishing guidance, approved use cases, education and training, so employees know where we’re heading and where to bring their questions. This also matters for compliance. Having an AI tool repository backed by one set of usage standards means we always know what’s running and why.

And sometimes, after all those checks, the answer is no. For example, one app jumped in costs unexpectedly and, when we realized our main AI platform could handle it anyway, we consolidated. We know what each tool is doing and stay clear-eyed about what it achieves relative to what it costs. And the process is ongoing: evaluating performance, aligning spend with business goals and when needed, declining it.

This last part is crucial. As Jay wrote in September, many of us have gotten swept up in the hype and forgotten that AI is a tool that requires a business case. Again, this isn’t about shutting down new ways of doing things, but giving visibility into where efforts are going, backed by a process that keeps costs from snowballing.

Tokens for the sake of tokens just isn’t sustainable. In the year ahead, “no” should be the most valuable word in your AI vocabulary, not because AI isn’t valuable, but because maximizing its value through meaningful constraint is.

item.title: The AI at the source of water management reform
item.description:
Korea Water Resources Corporation, better known as K-water, serves as sort of a water wholesaler, managing water in dams, treating it at purification plants, and supplying it to local municipalities. Now, the company is using AI to transform how to connect the flow of water from one end to the other.

K-water has a long history of using technology to operate dams. In the past, however, it relied largely on historical climate patterns and operating experience accumulated over many years. As climate change brings more frequent and unexpected extremes of rainfall and drought, more situations are proving difficult to predict using those methods. So K-water needed new tools for analysis and forecasting, and AI was the answer.

Source of the matter

Flood damage downstream of dams in 2020 prompted K-water to begin adopting AI and digital twin technology in earnest. To extend that work across the organization, it established the AI Division in late 2025, which brings together internal specialists from a range of disciplines, including IT, administration, civil engineering, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, environmental engineering, and telecommunications.

Its task is to bring technologies developed in separate areas — including digital twins for water management, AI-powered treatment plants, and smart water distribution network management — into a single framework. That framework spans the entire process of managing water in dams, treating it, and delivering it to users.

Ha-Dong Jung, VP of K-water’s AI division, joined in 1997 and became its first head. He’s witnessed its IT evolution firsthand, and to him, the division’s creation was a natural progression. K-water has consistently used technology to drive internal innovation, and AI is a continuation of that work.

Data management has been a particular focus. Initially, K-water collected information on dam levels, rainfall and water quality mainly for monitoring. It later began using that data to forecast water demand and plan production and supply. Through initiatives such as its ERP implementation, it also refined its metadata and data standards. Those efforts weren’t undertaken with AI in mind, but the foundations they established allowed K-water to begin AI projects ahead of others, and now they underpin the AI Division’s work. Collecting large amounts of data, however, didn’t make it immediately ready for AI.

“In the past, the purpose of our data work was to collect and store data and display it so people could understand it at a glance,” Jung says. “Today, that accumulated data is just a collection of numbers. To use it for AI, we need to define what each piece of data means and how the different data points relate to one another.”

Understanding how rain upstream of a dam affects water quality and output at a treatment plant, and ultimately the water supply, requires connecting data from multiple facilities. K-water is therefore investing in an ontology that defines data concepts and their relationships. It’s also combining this with RAG to build a system that can find and use the information needed.

Not always calm waters

There’ve been practical obstacles, says Jung. Attempts to extract large volumes of data for analysis sometimes caused existing equipment to stop working. K-water had to improve its collection infrastructure, including adding multiple routes for acquiring data.

“The existing equipment was designed with specifications suited to its original tasks,” he adds. “It wasn’t built to accommodate the extraction of the large volumes of data that AI projects require. Sometimes we’d be told things were working, only to check and find that the process had stopped partway through. We’re working internally to address those issues.”

To bring scattered data together and use it more efficiently, K-water has secured a site in Sejong for an AI data center, which it aims to build by 2030.

Bringing workplace AI up to employee standards

Alongside its facility operations, K-water is changing the AI tools available to employees. It has actively explored ways to provide external services alongside AI services developed in-house. As a public enterprise, it faces constraints on adopting external services quickly, but it’s worked through those restrictions step by step.

K-water first built an internal service called K-water GPT using Meta’s Llama models, improving performance by replacing the underlying models over time. But there were limits to how closely an in-house service could keep pace with rapidly advancing external AI offerings.

“Employees already judge AI against global services such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude,” Jung says. “It’s difficult to keep up with the pace of development in global AI models through in-house development alone, so we introduced external services that allow employees to choose among major AI models as needed in an environment with enhanced security.”

Further improvements followed. Because its internal work network and internet network are separate, employees faced limitations in using internal documents with AI. K-water began working on connections that would make external generative AI services available from the internal work network as well.

Growing adoption also brought the challenge of managing costs. Initially, K-water allowed broad use to encourage employees to try the tools. It now sets individual usage limits.

One unresolved challenge is the gap between the pace of technological change and the time it takes to execute projects. According to Jung, an IT project typically takes six months to a year to prepare, about a year to implement, and another six months or so to close out. AI models and capabilities continue to change throughout that period as well.

“Things have changed by the time you finish preparing, and they change again while you’re working your way through implementation,” he says. “Over the longer term, I think we may need to create an environment where our own employees can respond directly, rather than continuing to rely entirely on outside contractors.”

Building that internal capability is no simple matter either. Securing staff and completing project reviews and budget assessments takes considerable time. Meanwhile, technology moves on, and how to adapt procedures to the pace of technology is a continuing challenge for the public sector.

Past efforts paving the way for progress

Public enterprises and agencies are often seen as slow to respond to technological change because of the procedures they must follow. Structural constraints do make it difficult to accelerate change. Yet K-water is regarded as one of South Korea’s leading public enterprises in AI. OpenAI has also highlighted it as a prime example of AI use in disaster response, drawing attention to its water management capabilities.

Jung attributes that progress to a willingness to embrace change and take on challenges that have become ingrained in K-water’s employees.

“Earlier in my career, I found it difficult to deal with frequent system changes,” he says. “If a project of high cost fell short of expectations, I considered it a failure. But over time, I saw the people who came after me build on the technology and experience from those projects, try again, and eventually deliver results. That’s when I realized that tech doesn’t end with a single attempt. Earlier efforts build on one another. I think K-water employees have that DNA of persisting and pushing ahead.”

That doesn’t mean repeating the same work. Advances in technology, shifts in organizational thinking, and changes in available resources can make previously difficult initiatives possible. K-water’s AI projects, too, were made possible by the operational data it had accumulated over many years.

Jung says the progress so far is only the beginning, with the company’s use of AI in the early stages.

A measure of success

The AI Division’s ultimate goal is to help establish K-water as a global water company leading the response to climate change. In pursuing that goal, Jung sees his role as helping employees continue to take on challenges. When they hit a wall, he examines the problem with them and looks first for obstacles he can remove as a leader.

“I need to start by asking whether there’s something I can do to help,” he says. “If it’s a problem I can resolve at my level, I do everything I can to resolve it. If it isn’t, I spend more time listening to what employees have to say.”

item.title: Cisco’s 4 pillars for achieving agentic AI transformation
item.description:
Cisco Systems, a giant in networking, cybersecurity, and AI, is leveraging a combination of agentic AI, traditional AI, and automation to transform its business from top to bottom.

Liz Centoni, EVP and chief customer experience officer, is at the helm of the company’s $15 billion services business, an organization of 20,000 employees responsible for professional services, customer success, technical support, and the renewals engine for software and services.

In 2024, she led the company’s $28 billion acquisition of Splunk. Today, the 26-year Cisco veteran is helping guide the multinational tech conglomerate’s transformation into an AI-native company in terms of internal operations and what it delivers to its customers.

At the heart of her vision are these governing ideas:

  • Every workflow constrained by human availability is a workflow for redesign.
  • The status quo is not an option. Customer expectations and demands will continue to grow. You can’t rest on your laurels because revenue is growing and margins look good, so you must continually consider and reimagine your processes and offerings.
  • The quality we have today is the floor, not the ceiling. The capabilities of AI continue to evolve at a rapid pace.
  • Leadership, not technology, is the limiting factor. Leaders need to find and support the leaders underneath them who can amplify efforts and bring people along with them.

Based on her experience, Centoni also has four pieces of advice to achieve success with agentic AI.

1. Change the cost equation of expertise

“We didn’t just start bolting on AI,” Centoni says. “We looked at the underlying workflows to understand how we could redo work.”

This was one of the first lessons Centoni and her team took to heart. When she took on her current position two years ago, she spent time looking through feedback from customers. One of the biggest pet peeves customers expressed was the frustration of the path leading to the right expert to solve a problem. That process frequently required handoffs from one engineer to another, and explaining the problem in detail each time.

The team’s first reaction was to build an agent that would speed up the process to find the right engineer to handle the problem. That, Centoni says, was a misstep.

“It just upset our customers more because it showed that we actually did five handoffs behind the scenes and it surfaced it to them faster,” Centoni says. “We just bolted AI onto the wrong thing and said, ‘automation.’”

Before even thinking about creating an agent, what they should’ve asked, Centoni says, was why have handoffs in the first place. It’s not enough to simply map a workflow and attempt to automate it because steps of that workflow may have been designed decades ago to address an issue an agent may not have or be able to cut through. It’s essential to understand the desired end result, and then design a workflow with current capabilities and constraints in mind, she adds.

“Users are an essential part of the technology stack,” Centoni says. “You have to bring in the subject matter experts and the users to outline the workflow, and you have to get close to the work. If you can’t, you have no right designing.”

An important element, she continues, is to carefully consider the boundaries between where an agent can do something autonomously and where it’s necessary to hand the process off to a human. Where can you use automation and AI with 90%-plus accuracy?

That gets you to start rethinking the workflow, Centoni says, since throughout most of Cisco’s history, the approach to customer engagements was to throw experts at a problem. The more complex the engagement, the more experts were needed. For customers, the priority was getting the job done correctly but as quickly as possible, yet the availability of expert engineers throttled Cisco’s ability to speed up the process.

 “When I came into this business, we treated every customer we had like a bespoke model,” Centoni says. “But over the last 40-plus years, we’ve solved these problems tens of thousands of times.”

Cisco has taken 40 years of engagements to build a knowledge base and a series of playbooks that AI agents and human experts can use to help customers plan and execute deployments. Cisco can now take the information they have about a customer, including their KPIs for a project, and customize its value realization without needing to include a lot of human experts on top.

“You go into a new deployment with an expert agent that brings in all the prior experts and democratizes the knowledge base,” Centoni says. “The outcome for the customer is consistency, security, and better time to project completion.”

Still, human experts are always in the loop, and Centoni says the team would have more bandwidth for conversations with the customer on how to iterate and help them feel they get more than what they paid for.

2. Be more proactive and predictive

“Over the years, our focus has always been on how fast we can get to root cause analysis of customer issues,” Centoni says. “If it took me three hours before, can I get it down to 30 minutes.”

Helping customers solve issues faster is admirable, but AI can help Cisco be more proactive and predictive. Instead of just speed, the company is now leaning on AI to help it stop issues before they hit a customer.

“When we look at case histories, we can see clusters that happen over and over again,” she says. Cisco leverages decades of understanding what can go wrong as a knowledge base. Agents can now continually monitor customer environments for anything that might signal an issue is occurring, and recommend next best steps before it becomes critical.

“In 12 months, I’d like to be able to sit down with a customer and say you would’ve had 10 outages last year and we prevented eight of them,” Centoni says.

3. Pick models and tools to fit the use case

While the past year has been all about AI adoption and token maxing, companies and their boards are increasingly paying attention to the ROI of their AI efforts and demanding results. The key to keeping costs down and returns high, Centoni says, is to be intentional about models and tools.

“Before we even go down the AI path, we ask, ‘Can automation do this?’” she says. “If it’s purely rules-based, I’m doing automation. If it requires bringing multiple signals together to drive a prediction, then AI. In many cases, it’s not binary. We have a combination of things where we use old predictive AI models, automation, and some of the newer LLMs.”

When an agent is called for, pick the models and tools that best fit the use case, not the preferences of the designer. For instance, a use case might involve data sovereignty requirements in which data must stay on prem.

“If you look at our AI assistant for renewals, which brings together a renewals agent, a sentiment agent, a risk agent, and an install base agent, it’s actually based on Mistral because they were one of the few who could give us an on-prem model that had the full capabilities,” Centoni says. “We customized that model using a private instance and we use automation along with it as well.”

4. Avoid compliance theater

A lot of tech leaders measure their AI success by adoption. Not Centoni. If you measure adoption, a lot of users will just check the box to say they’ve used it, and then use the old processes and tools to get the actual work done. Centoni calls it compliance theater.

If she wants to understand the success of the AI Cisco has deployed, she sees if the workflows have changed, and if the renewals team demonstrated greater capacity since the AI assistant for renewals was deployed. That’s a much more telling metric for measuring success.

To truly get users to engage with AI, you must understand that agents are a continuous work in progress and they make users an integral part of the feedback loop as you iterate.

“The difference between an agent and a piece of software is with software, you build, test, deploy it, and it’s 100% feature complete,” Centoni says. “With an agent, it’s 60% of the way there in its first iteration in terms of usability, and the user is part of the tech stack that gives us feedback.”

A good channel for that feedback is essential, she adds, because you can only make an agent usable at scale when you get that feedback and continue to iterate.

For example, Cisco’s internal support agent runs seamlessly in the support workflow. As soon as a customer opens a case, the agent pulls in all of the customer’s relevant history and context so a support worker instantly has it at their fingertips, rather than spending the first 30 minutes with a customer asking for details of what went wrong.

“That’s a lot of time and frustration saved up front,” Centoni says. “It also provides the next best action. Now a support team member can help the customer and recommend things based on what is known about their environment.”

item.title: Your AI ROI problem is a culture problem
item.description:
These days, when I talk to CIOs about how their organizations are using AI, there’s a lot less excitement about new tools and the potential for higher productivity, and a lot more anxiety about what the return on investment has been so far. Because for most companies, that return has been less than expected, especially as cost per token is increasing.

Last year, IBM’s 2025 CEO study found that only 25% of AI initiatives had delivered the expected ROI over the last few years, and only 16% had scaled enterprise-wide. MIT’s NANDA initiative found that 95% of generative AI pilots delivered no measurable P&L (profit and loss) impact. More recently, SAP and Oxford Economics’ Value of AI Report 2026 found that 69% of businesses worldwide are “satisfied” with the ROI of their AI costs – but more than two-thirds think there’s still room for improvement.

It’s tempting to read those numbers as a verdict on AI’s limitations. But the research points somewhere else. When Boston Consulting Group surveyed 1,000 senior executives, it found roughly 70% of AI implementation challenges stemmed from people and processes, 20% from technology and 10% from the algorithms themselves.

The companies seeing the most value from AI? They were investing 10% in algorithms, 20% in technology and data, and 70% in people and processes.

As CIO, you don’t just own the tools. You lead the teams that determine whether the tools pay off.

My own experience with AI – integrating it into Per Scholas’s classrooms, systems and processes to achieve even stronger outcomes for our learners – has convinced me that there are three cultural traits separating teams that produce returns from teams that produce pilots: they are results-oriented, entrepreneurial and collegial.

Start with the result, and measure progress

Decide what you’re trying to change before choosing what to invest in. McKinsey’s 2025 State of AI survey found that while 80% of companies set efficiency as an objective for their AI initiatives, the companies seeing the most value often set growth or innovation as additional objectives. Those high performers are nearly three times as likely to report fundamentally redesigned individual workflows, and that redesign was among the strongest contributors to business impact of all the factors McKinsey tested.

Leaders are also getting more realistic about timelines. In TEKsystems’ State of Digital Transformation 2026 report, only 27% of organizations expected transformation ROI within six months, down from 42% a year earlier. That’s a good thing. It gives CIOs room to measure honestly instead of declaring early victories.

In practice, every AI project needs a named owner, a baseline and a business metric before it starts. If you can’t say what “better” looks like in numbers, you won’t be able to prove you got there. When we built ResumeBoost, a tool to help our alumni strengthen their resumes, our first measure was time. It cut the time staff spent working with alumni on their resumes by over a third and ensured alumni were aligning their skills and experiences with their target roles.

But measuring honestly means tracking more than one number, and being willing to act on what the different metrics tell you.

Make it safe to try, and to fail small

If you focus on results but don’t provide room to experiment, your teams will only invest in safe bets. AI rewards the opposite. A 2025 MIT Technology Review Insights survey found that 83% of business leaders believe “experiment-friendly cultures” make AI initiatives much more likely to succeed, yet 22% had hesitated to lead AI projects for fear of failure or criticism.

Hands-on experimentation isn’t a distraction from results. It’s how teams build the judgment to deliver them. And that entrepreneurial energy is most likely already in your organization. MIT’s researchers found a “shadow AI” economy in which employees are using personal AI tools even when official pilots stall. Their prescription included moving from central labs to empowered teams. The question for CIOs is whether that initiative happens inside your governance or around it.

ResumeBoost is a good example of failing small. The time savings were real, but the user experience for alumni didn’t hit the mark. Rather than keep it as a standalone tool, we folded its functionality into the broader AI coaching platform used by learners. The pilot did its job: it showed enough promise to warrant further investment, and it told us where to pivot.

At Per Scholas, that entrepreneurial energy comes from people with deep institutional knowledge. Ed Hernandez, who designed our AI-Native Classroom, has been part of the Per Scholas community for roughly fifteen years. He started as a learner and later became an instructor. Then, after more than a decade of leading our curriculum and instructional development team, Ed’s passion for AI and software products led us to create an AI solutions team and ask him to lead it. He knows where the real pain points are because he’s seen them from both sides of the classroom.

For the AI-Native Classroom, leadership’s job was to say yes, set clear guardrails and remove obstacles. But the biggest task for us was to weigh possibility against necessity. The AI-Native Classroom earned support not only because the ideas were compelling, but because they solved problems our instructors and learners actually had.

That’s the entrepreneurial culture I’d urge every CIO to build: authorize initiative, bound the risk, tie experiments to the mission and reward the people who try.

And the classroom is only part of the picture. A significant share of our AI work is staff-facing, built for the teams who run our programs and connect graduates with employers. The same principles apply there.

Candor helps, too. People don’t experiment freely with a technology they suspect could soon replace them. Be transparent about what the goals are, and what it would mean for your organization to achieve them.

Build collegial, cross-functional teams

AI can’t replace collaboration. What it can do is make collaboration more valuable by bridging silos.

The companies pulling ahead treat collaboration as infrastructure. Accenture’s research on “Talent Reinventors,” organizations that advance people and AI together, found they delivered revenue growth 1.8 percentage points higher and profit growth 1.4 points higher than peers in 2025.

Collegiality means pairing technologists with the people who own the workflow, rather than delivering tools to them. We built our AI-Native Classroom with our instructors, not for them. We took the same approach with Sherlock, a job-sourcing tool our AI team built with the staff who connect our graduates with employers.

Finding roles for learners used to mean opening a dozen job boards, rerunning the same searches and weeding out staffing firms’ reposts of the same opening. Sherlock now reviews more than 125,000 postings a day and delivers one feed of roles that match our training tracks and each campus’s recruiting footprint.

But it was designed around how that team already works. Saved roles go on a list shared across each campus, so one colleague’s find becomes everyone’s lead, and they export in a format built for the Salesforce job orders staff already create. Staff also tune the feed themselves by flagging roles that don’t belong and ones they know exist but never appeared. Three weeks after launch, staff at nearly three-quarters of our campuses had logged in, weekly users had more than doubled and users saved more than 100 hours they would otherwise have spent sourcing jobs.

Seven weeks in, those same staff are telling us where Sherlock falls short, and we’re now scoping out the enhancements they’ve asked for. It’s an early success, not a finished story. Staying successful requires incremental implementation driven by an open dialogue between the people who build the tools and the people who use them.

The talent you hire is the culture you get

None of this requires a new platform. It requires CIOs to treat culture as part of the AI investment. AI is a force amplifier, not a force generator: it magnifies whatever already exists in a team. With a strong culture, AI becomes an extension of what makes an organization distinctive. With a weak one, the same problems surface, only faster.

Culture also shapes who you hire and how you develop them.

The employers we work with increasingly see talent as something to build, not just buy. As Equinix’s chief people officer put it when describing the company’s investment in early-career pathways, “We’re not just competing for talent; we’re creating it.” When we prepare learners for high-growth careers, technical skills are the baseline. What employers tell us sets people apart is whether they can define a problem, try something new and work across a team to solve it.

Those are the same traits that decide whether your AI budget becomes a line item or a return.

item.title: Microsoft struggles to get M365 services back online after widespread outage
item.description:
Editor’s note: Microsoft has announced that it has fixed the underlying issue for the outage and is restoring services to customers.

If you’re struggling to send or receive emails, you’re not alone. Microsoft has been unable to fully restore Microsoft 365 more than 13 hours after an Exchange Online failure took down Outlook and spread to Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and parts of the company’s security tooling, and it said overnight that its latest fixes were “not taking as expected.”

The outage began at 16:17 UTC on Nov. 12, according to Microsoft’s service health dashboard.

“Users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop (MAPI), Exchange ActiveSync (EAS), or REST-based connections, and email delivery may be delayed,” Microsoft wrote in the dashboard.

Users in the Americas could not reach their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop Outlook, mobile clients, or the REST API. Within two hours, Microsoft said users in any region could be affected. It opened a wider incident covering Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot, Defender XDR, Intune, Power BI, and several Purview services.

Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak.

In its latest service-health updates for incident MO1550821, Microsoft said it had observed a surge in calls from routing services to backend servers as it applied mitigation measures. The company said traffic rebalancing had contributed to the increased volume and that it was scaling virtual machines to add capacity and reduce the load.

“As we’ve applied our current ongoing mitigation actions, we’ve observed a surge in outbound call volume from our routing services to our backend servers,” Microsoft said in the update. It added: “We’re continuing to observe heightened volume due to traffic rebalancing actions that we have taken throughout this event.”

Server failures behind the disruption

Microsoft initially investigated elevated infrastructure load and the possibility that a recent change had contributed to the incident. It later said the problem was not being driven by an overall increase in traffic.

“We’ve determined that the elevated load isn’t driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure,” the company said in its Exchange Online incident update.

In a subsequent update, Microsoft identified a process responsible for establishing secure connections as a source of the problem.

“Our investigation has found that a process on the affected servers responsible for establishing secure connections becomes overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop processing requests,” the company said.

Microsoft said it was preparing a configuration change to address the behaviour and testing it on a subset of servers before wider deployment. It was also reverting a recent network configuration change that correlated with the start of the disruption, while restarting affected infrastructure and monitoring server stability.

The recovery process has involved restricting some traffic and gradually reintroducing connections as Microsoft checks whether servers can remain stable under load. The company also reported that some servers became unresponsive again after traffic was restored, requiring further analysis and mitigation.

Impact extends beyond email

Microsoft’s incident notification said the impact varied by service and feature, depending in part on whether they relied on Exchange Online.

The company said users might be unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes through Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop, Exchange ActiveSync, or REST-based connections, and that email delivery might be delayed. It said Teams’ core messaging and online meetings remained largely functional, but Exchange-dependent features such as calendar access and meeting scheduling could fail.

Microsoft also said that direct access to files stored in SharePoint Online remained functional, while features dependent on Exchange Online could be affected. For Microsoft 365 Copilot, users might be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses, and Copilot experiences might be unable to access work data such as email, calendars, and files.

The notification also identified potential impacts to Defender for Office 365 Safe Links, which might be unable to verify URLs clicked in Outlook and Teams, and to some Defender XDR portal pages. Other reported impacts included selected Intune device enrolment and compliance scenarios and Purview functions such as data loss prevention, automatic labelling and communication compliance.

Enterprise concentration risk

The incident has renewed attention on the operational dependencies created when organisations consolidate email, collaboration and security functions within a single cloud ecosystem.

“Enterprises have priced Microsoft 365 as a licence and never as a single point of failure,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research.

Gogia said that when mail, meetings and security functions such as Safe Links depend on the same service estate, an infrastructure disruption can affect several business functions at once.

“The answer is not a second suite. It is a rehearsed fallback for the few things that cannot stop: an out-of-band channel for incident command, mail continuity for critical roles, and a written decision on whether each security control fails open or closed,” he said.

For security teams, the distinction between a service being unavailable and a dependent security function being impaired is important. Microsoft’s notification about Safe Links, for example, points to a specific URL-verification impact rather than the loss of all Defender for Office 365 capabilities.

Gogia also said enterprise customers would want a detailed account of the incident, including a timeline showing when Microsoft identified the different causes and how it validated the recovery measures. Microsoft has continued to publish updates through its Microsoft 365 service status portal. The company has not yet published a final post-incident root-cause report.
